validation_note: Every case in this batch is supported by an official or public institutional source. Analogies are management lessons, not automatic diagnoses for Olszówka/Gardeja.

cases.name: Lake Balkhash
cases.observed_pattern: Lake Balkhash has no surface outlet and depends heavily on the Ili River. NASA reports gradual shrinkage as water is diverted from feeder rivers for agriculture, hydropower and industry, while evaporation remains a major loss.
cases.management_lesson: For an endorheic lake, feeder-river continuity and upstream withdrawals must be monitored together with evaporation; a visible lake can be losing resilience long before complete desiccation.

provenance.title: A Delta Oasis in Southeastern Kazakhstan
provenance.supports: Significant Ili River water is diverted for dams and irrigation, creating vulnerability for the Ili delta and Lake Balkhash system.

cases.name: Tonle Sap
cases.observed_pattern: Tonle Sap depends on the seasonal reversal of the Tonle Sap River driven by high Mekong levels; UNESCO reports that the lake can expand up to fivefold in the rainy season and is under pressure from infrastructure development, over-exploitation and climate change.
cases.management_lesson: Hydrologic direction, timing and floodplain connectivity can matter as much as annual water volume. Monitoring should detect whether a seasonal pulse arrives, how long it lasts and how far the floodplain reconnects.

provenance.title: Promoting Environmental Conservation at Tonle Sap Biosphere Reserve
provenance.supports: The Mekong-driven reverse flow expands the lake up to five times and the system faces infrastructure, over-exploitation and climate pressures.

cases.name: Lake Naivasha / Malewa wetland
cases.observed_pattern: UNEP reports that flooding incised the Malewa River bed so deeply that seasonal overflow into the river-mouth wetland stopped and the wetland fell from about 1,350 to 450 hectares. UNEP also reports pollution and over-extraction pressure on Lake Naivasha.
cases.management_lesson: A channel becoming deeper can drain water past a wetland rather than into it. Elevation differences, bankfull thresholds and overflow paths should be mapped when a shallow wetland disappears while the main river remains present.

provenance.title: Kenya’s wetlands: a financing challenge
provenance.supports: Malewa riverbed incision stopped seasonal overflow and reduced the wetland from roughly 1,350 ha to 450 ha, removing a natural sediment and nutrient filter.

provenance.title: Putting the Spotlight on Lake Naivasha this World Water Day
provenance.supports: Lake Naivasha experienced dramatic low levels and increasing pressure from pollution and over-extraction.

cases.name: Inle Lake
cases.observed_pattern: UNESCO describes heavy impacts from pollution and sedimentation around Inle Lake and reports that expansion of floating gardens accounted for most of a roughly one-third reduction in open-water area since 1935, while agrochemicals contribute to eutrophication.
cases.management_lesson: Apparent shoreline loss can be caused by land conversion and sediment accumulation rather than only drought. Water-extent monitoring should be paired with land-cover change and turbidity or vegetation indicators.

provenance.title: Indawgyi Lake Wildlife Sanctuary — comparison with Inle Lake
provenance.supports: Inle Lake has heavy pollution and sedimentation impacts; floating gardens are linked to most of the one-third reduction in open-water area since 1935 and agrochemical eutrophication.

cases.name: Lake Tana / Tana-Beles sub-basins
cases.observed_pattern: The World Bank identifies degrading watersheds, floods, droughts, unsustainable fisheries and unplanned development as major Tana-Beles challenges, while reporting restoration of more than 70,000 hectares of degraded watershed and modernization of monitoring and flood warning.
cases.management_lesson: Lake management improves when the upstream catchment is treated as infrastructure. Erosion control, restoration and hydrometeorological monitoring should be evaluated alongside the lake surface itself.

provenance.title: World Bank Provides Additional financing for the Development of Tana and Beles Sub-Basins in Ethiopia
provenance.supports: The project addressed degraded watersheds, flood/drought risks and weak monitoring; over 70,000 ha of watershed were restored and hydrometeorological monitoring was modernized.

cases.name: Lake Sevan
cases.observed_pattern: The World Bank reports that over-extraction in areas including Lake Sevan threatens agriculture and drinking supplies. It also identifies forests as important for reducing sediment delivery to Lake Sevan, protecting water quality and helping stabilize lake levels.
cases.management_lesson: Quantity and catchment condition interact: abstraction control should be combined with erosion and sediment management rather than treated as separate problems.

provenance.title: Climate Action in Armenia Can Deliver Cleaner Air, Healthier Communities, and Stronger Economic Growth
provenance.supports: Armenia faces high water stress and over-extraction in areas including Lake Sevan.

provenance.title: Preserving Forests is Key to Armenia’s Climate Goals and Economic Sustainability
provenance.supports: Forest cover reduces sediment deposition into Lake Sevan, supports water quality and helps stabilize water levels.

cases.name: Ichkeul Lake and marshes
cases.observed_pattern: UNESCO reports that upstream dams cut off nearly all freshwater flow, increased salinity and degraded the wetland. Recovery followed water-control restoration, planned freshwater releases and monitoring; the site was removed from the Danger List in 2006.
cases.management_lesson: When upstream storage disconnects a wetland, environmental water requirements can be quantified and managed explicitly. Restoration needs both controlled inflow and downstream exchange management, not just a one-time refill.

provenance.title: Case Study: Ichkeul National Park (Tunisia)
provenance.supports: Upstream dams cut freshwater flow; management now regulates freshwater releases and saltwater exchange with scientific monitoring.

provenance.title: Ichkeul National Park
provenance.supports: The site was placed on the Danger List due to dam-related freshwater impacts and removed in 2006 after improvement and progressing ecosystem restoration.

cases.name: Kissimmee River
cases.observed_pattern: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers reports that the meandering Kissimmee River was dredged into the deep C-38 canal between 1962 and 1971. Restoration backfills canal reaches, removes control structures and re-establishes river-floodplain wetland conditions.
cases.management_lesson: A deep straight channel can move water efficiently while destroying floodplain storage and ecological connectivity. Restoration can require raising hydraulic residence time and reconnecting historic channels, but only through engineered, monitored projects.

provenance.publisher: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Jacksonville District
provenance.title: Kissimmee River Restoration Project
provenance.supports: The river was channelized into C-38; the restoration targets river channel and floodplain wetland reconnection.

cases.name: Lake Erie — western basin nutrients
cases.observed_pattern: The U.S. EPA identifies phosphorus delivered by tributaries, especially the Maumee River, as a key driver of western Lake Erie harmful algal blooms and hypoxia. U.S. and Canadian programs target phosphorus reductions and adaptive monitoring.
cases.management_lesson: Stable lake area does not imply healthy water. Nutrient flux from tributaries, rainfall-driven loading and bloom response must be included in a water-management system alongside water quantity.

provenance.title: Lake Erie Water Quality Data
provenance.supports: Western Lake Erie is highly eutrophic; spring soluble phosphorus from the Maumee River is a strong predictor of harmful algal bloom severity.

provenance.title: Lake Erie Nutrients
provenance.supports: The United States and Canada are working to reduce phosphorus entering Lake Erie to limit harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen zones.

cases.name: Hula wetland / Hula Nature Reserve
cases.observed_pattern: Israel Nature and Parks Authority describes the historic drainage of Hula Lake and a later approximately two-metre elevation difference that disconnected the reserve from the Jordan system. Recent restoration rewetted part of the reserve and created a fish passage to renew hydraulic connectivity.
cases.management_lesson: Small elevation changes created by drainage or erosion can sever connectivity even when two water systems remain close on a map. Terrain elevation, channel-bed level and reconnection thresholds should be measured directly.

provenance.title: Hula Nature Reserve
provenance.supports: The reserve contains a restored remnant of historic Hula Lake and documents the large twentieth-century drainage project.

provenance.title: Fish ladders and barrier removal: fish upstream to the Hula Reserve
provenance.supports: Drainage-induced erosion created about a two-metre level difference and hydraulic disconnection; rewetting and a fish passage were used to restore connectivity.
